clue.text: Hardened heart — the mark of a tyrant

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letters, here the middle pair of the eight-letter word Hardened

parts.note: a mark or blemish is a spot

explanation.surface: A tyrant is known by his callous, hardened heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardened heart' reads as a description of the tyrant, but 'heart' asks for the middle letters of 'Hardened', DE.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name an absolute ruler who governs cruelly.

clue.text: OT character set up one church

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the word is written upwards, so reversed

parts.note: taken as the word itself

explanation.surface: An Old Testament figure founded a church.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'set up' means written upwards; 'OT character' means a figure from the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Enoch, father of Methuselah, is a figure in Genesis, part of the Old Testament.

parts.note: not a machine for someone called Walker but a device that computes how far a pedestrian has gone by counting steps

explanation.surface: A computer belonging to someone named Walker.
explanation.definitionFit: The device counts a hiker's paces and so reckons the distance travelled.

indicators.note: the initial of a word is its opening letter, here taken from Tom's

parts.note: a blunder is an error

explanation.surface: Tom's first mistake throws everyone into panic.
explanation.definitionFit: Terror is extreme fear, a state close to panic.

clue.text: Vanquished the enemy, as Sir Henry did ?

parts.note: to vanquish is to beat
time is called the enemy in the old saying 'time is the enemy'

explanation.surface: A knight defeated his foes in battle.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Henry is Sir Henry Wood, the conductor who founded the Proms, the London summer concert season; a conductor marks the rhythm with a baton.
explanation.definitionFit: A conductor keeps the musical pulse by marking it with his baton, as Wood did.

definitions.meaning: three snaps, each one a fracture
the title of Tennyson's lyric that opens 'on thy cold gray stones, O Sea'

explanation.definitionFit: A snap is a fracture, so three of them repeated give the poem's title, a lament by the sea.

parts.note: 16 is an allusion or citation; the little star printed in text sends the reader to a footnote

explanation.surface: A celebrity worth noting.
explanation.walkthrough: The 16 points to 16-down, REFERENCE: the starred mark refers the reader to a note.
explanation.definitionFit: The typographic symbol's name comes from Greek for little star, and it marks a cross-reference to a footnote.

parts.note: Shakespeare's seven ages speech describes the soldier as full of strange oaths; here a body of such soldiers

explanation.surface: Soldiers who swear in strange ways.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Jaques's 'All the world's a stage' speech in As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of soldiers, a cavalry or armoured company, is a group of the oath-swearing men described.

clue.text: Force relay of workers to supply substitute

parts.note: to force someone is to make them
a shift is a group of workers taking its turn

explanation.surface: Bosses compel a team of replacement workers to fill in.
explanation.definitionFit: A makeshift is a temporary stand-in used for want of anything better.

clue.text: Surprise for the foreign 'people in town assembly

indicators.note: the foreign word and people go inside the rearranged town
an assembly puts parts together in a new order, so the letters of town are rearranged

parts.note: der is German for the
men are people

explanation.surface: Foreign visitors cause surprise at a town meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'assembly' rearranges the word town, and 'in' places the German article and the people inside that rearrangement; 'Surprise' looks like a verb but is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Wonderment is astonishment, the feeling of being amazed.

definitions.meaning: one of the five Classics, the major English flat horse races, run at Epsom

explanation.definitionFit: The Oaks is an Epsom race for fillies, and the same word names broad-leaved trees.

clue.text: Pretended to sway the growth of Ireland

parts.note: sham describes something pretended or fake
to rock is to sway

explanation.surface: Someone faked swaying to Irish music.
explanation.definitionFit: The three-leaved clover is the national emblem of Ireland.

clue.text: Rest take up a fresh attitude?

explanation.definitionFit: Repose means relaxation, and split as re-pose it means to strike a new posture.

parts.note: S is south, one of the four quarters of the compass
docked means cut short

explanation.surface: A section is cut off an animal's tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'docked from tail' sounds like tail-docking, but the tail is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A scut is the short tail of a rabbit, hare or deer.

definitions.meaning: a single written symbol, as in the Greek alphabet
a person in a work of fiction

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a written symbol and a figure in a story.

parts.note: sappers are the Royal Engineers, RE, and the possessive adds S
a train is a means of transport

explanation.surface: Keep back the army engineers' vehicles.
explanation.definitionFit: To restrain is to check or keep under control.

clue.text: Allusion concerning criminal is made without hesitation

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside, so the criminal surrounds the hesitation

parts.note: a fence is a criminal who handles stolen goods
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A remark about a criminal is made without pausing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' reads as 'lacking', but here it keeps its old sense of outside: the receiver of stolen goods goes around the hesitation sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A reference is a mention of something, an allusion to it.

clue.text: Cake is the wrong one — upset everybody

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means the word is turned upside down, so reversed

parts.note: all means everybody

explanation.surface: A cake is the wrong kind and everyone is annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns ALL into LLA at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A tortilla is a flat unleavened maize or wheat bread, loosely a cake.

indicators.note: an adaptation reworks the material, so the letters are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A performer appears in the film version of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adaptation' rearranges ACTOR IN A; 'novel' looks like it describes the adaptation but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Catriona is Robert Louis Stevenson's sequel to Kidnapped.

clue.text: A lot put in half a teacup ?

indicators.note: the answer is put in, so sits inside, the run of letters across the words half a teacup

explanation.surface: Someone pours a large amount into a half-filled teacup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot' looks like a quantity of tea, but it is the definition, in the sense of one's lot in life.
explanation.definitionFit: One's lot is one's destiny, the portion life deals out.

indicators.note: the reluctant word is to be put aboard the ship, sitting between its letters

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, so being shipped is being placed inside SS
loth means unwilling or reluctant

explanation.surface: Creatures that dislike being transported by sea.
explanation.walkthrough: LOTH goes inside SS, the steamship abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloths are slow tree-dwelling mammals of South America.

clue.text: Hardy character, Jack brought back hound

indicators.note: the two pieces are read in reverse order and backwards

parts.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles is Thomas Hardy's heroine
a jack is a sailor, abbreviated AB for able seaman

explanation.surface: A sailor in a Hardy novel returns with a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' reverses TESSAB as a whole, giving BASSET.
explanation.definitionFit: A basset is a short-legged scent hound.

clue.text: Pay by quarter to eight, perhaps

parts.note: S is south, one of the four quarters of the compass
a rowing eight is one example of a crew

explanation.surface: Workers are paid at a quarter to eight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarter to eight' looks like a time; it is S plus CREW. Screw is British slang for wages.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a screw is a salary or wage.

clue.text: Line used to make a toll-call ?

definitions.text: Line used to make a toll-call ?

parts.words: Line used to make a toll-call ?
parts.note: not a telephone line for a paid call but a cord pulled to make a church bell toll

explanation.surface: A telephone line for paying calls.
explanation.definitionFit: The cord hanging in a belfry is pulled to swing and sound the bell.

definitions.meaning: a kind of beast, the black-and-white bamboo eater
a British police car, named for its blue-and-white livery

explanation.definitionFit: The animal is a Chinese bear, and the name was also used for British police patrol cars.

indicators.note: lacking its finish, the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a beginning is a start

explanation.surface: An actor just starting out lacks polish.
explanation.definitionFit: A star is a leading performer.

indicators.note: to dish is to ruin or wreck, so the letters are wrecked into a new order

explanation.surface: A meal is eaten while waiting for an officer to arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish' looks like the food; it is the anagram signal working on EATEN UNTIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A lieutenant is a junior commissioned officer.

definitions.meaning: Artemus Ward was an American humorist, so read the word draw backwards to get his surname

explanation.definitionFit: A drawback is a snag, and draw read in reverse gives Ward, a humorist's surname.

clue.text: Board on which one declines to give another a rise

definitions.text: Board on which one declines to give another a rise

parts.words: Board on which one declines to give another a rise
parts.note: not a company board refusing a pay increase but a plank where one rider going down lifts the other

explanation.surface: A company board where one member refuses a colleague a pay increase.
explanation.definitionFit: A playground plank pivots in the middle, so as one end drops the other lifts.
